idiom_name: raise at the boundary (EAFP): exceptions abort the operation immediately; assert for internal invariants only
implementation_notes: In Python the fail-fast mechanism is the raise statement: check the precondition at the entry of the function and raise before any state is touched, so the traceback carries the origin and the caller gets a typed exception to classify. assert is the separate internal-invariant tool and is removed when the interpreter runs with -O, so it must never validate input or capacity. The EAFP style - try the operation and handle the specific exception - is fail-fast at the point of use, and it composes with context managers (with/ExitStack), which guarantee release on the failure path; bare except: clauses and except Exception handlers that log and continue are what turn it into fail-slow.
pitfalls: assert statements are stripped under python -O (and by some packagers), so an assertion-based guard silently disappears in production - use explicit raises for input and capacity checks.
An except Exception handler that returns a default value, or a bare except: pass, hides the failure; fail-fast code re-raises or lets the exception escape to the process boundary.
Mutations that already happened before the raise are not rolled back: a partially updated dict, file or database row is the classic fail-slow remainder, so guards belong before the first mutation.
